title: Recursive teaching dimension conjecture
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(K>0\) such that, for every finite set \(X\) and every finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\), \[\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)\leq K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)?\] Both dimensions are the combinatorial quantities defined below. The constant must be independent of the number of concepts, the domain size and the class itself.
why: A universal linear bound would connect sample-based combinatorial complexity with the number of examples needed for structured teaching. It asks whether recursive teaching can always be controlled at the same scale as VC dimension.
status_note: The conjecture is explicitly open in the 2023 source and the checked 2025 work. A bounded later-work search through 14 September 2026 found no general linear upper bound or unbounded-ratio counterexample. The new results address special classes and particular construction rules.

category_assignment.reason: The conjecture compares two dimensions of a concept class.

importance.reason: A fundamental proposed relationship between two established learning-complexity measures, with a general quadratic bound and an unresolved universal linear target.

sentences: A finite concept class can be studied through both its VC dimension and its recursive teaching dimension.
VC dimension measures the ability to realize label patterns, while recursive teaching measures how examples can identify concepts through successive elimination.
The question asks whether one universal constant always bounds recursive teaching dimension by that constant times VC dimension.
The same constant must work for every finite class.
The project seeks a direct quantitative link between the complexity of learning from samples and the information needed for structured teaching.

context_blocks.text: Simon’s 2023 Open Problem 3 asks for precisely this universal linear relationship. The earlier Simon–Zilles open-problem paper is retained as provenance from the already consolidated duplicate; there is a single active target.

VC dimension measures how freely a class can realize labels on a chosen set of instances. Teaching instead allows examples tailored to one concept. Recursive teaching measures the hardest easiest-to-teach concept that remains after restricting the candidate class; it is not the maximum ordinary teaching dimension of the original class.

Hu, Wu, Li and Wang prove \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=O(\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)^2)\). This bounds teaching complexity by VC dimension alone but leaves open whether the dependence can always be linear.
Simon’s 2025 paper verifies the conjecture for graph-induced star classes and graph-induced connected-set classes. These positive results cover rich families but not arbitrary Boolean classes.

Compton, Pabbaraju and Zhivotovskiy give lower bounds for particular greedy teaching-set constructions in 2025. They describe the universal conjecture as unresolved; limitations of those constructions are not counterexamples to the existence of small teaching sets.

The conjecture permits any universal constant, so examples separating the two dimensions by a fixed factor are compatible with it. Its failure would require ratios with no finite upper bound, while an affirmative result would uniformly connect two distinct notions of information needed for learning.

The 2023 question explicitly cites the 2015 source. Non-clashing teaching and sample compression remain different targets.

definitions: A concept is a function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\); repeated copies are not distinct concepts. A set \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every Boolean labelling of \(S\) is the restriction of some member of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the largest size of a shattered set, with value zero for the empty class. For a nonempty subclass \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C\) and \(h\in\mathcal D\), put \[t(h,\mathcal D)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \forall g\in\mathcal D,\ g|_S=h|_S\Rightarrow g=h\}.\] These are labelled teaching examples: the labels are those assigned by \(h\). The minimum exists, and for a singleton class it is zero. Set \(t_{\min}(\mathcal D)=\min_{h\in\mathcal D}t(h,\mathcal D)\), and define \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=\max_{\varnothing\ne\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C}t_{\min}(\mathcal D)\), with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\varnothing)=0\). Equivalently, repeatedly remove all concepts of minimum teaching-set size from the current class and take the largest such minimum encountered. No computational-efficiency, random-sampling or teacher-algorithm requirement is imposed. Restricting to finite \(X\) loses no instance for finite concept classes on an arbitrary domain: retain one domain point for each distinct vector of labels across the class. This preserves both dimensions and yields a finite domain.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal linear bound for some finite \(K\), or of its negation. A refutation must establish that for every \(K>0\) there is a finite class of positive VC dimension with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)>K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)\); one class with \(\operatorname{RTD}>\operatorname{VCdim}\) only rules out constant one. The optimal constant need not be determined. A quadratic upper bound, a result for special concept classes, or a lower bound for one teaching-set construction does not resolve the statement.
